fetched_contents.text: Early Thrombolysis and Outcomes in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Abstract BACKGROUND: This individual participant data meta-analysis aimed to determine whether time to treatment influences the effect of intraarterial thrombolysis (IAT), intravenous thrombolysis, and conservative standard therapy on visual outcomes in nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, CENTRAL, and Embase up to June 2023 for studies reporting treatment modality and peri-treatment best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) for ≥5 participants, excluding patients with nonsevere vision loss (BCVA <1.0 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution [logMAR]) or treated after 24 hours of symptom onset. The primary outcome was recovery from severe vision loss (final BCVA <1.0 logMAR). We used mixed-effect models and local polynomial regression to investigate nonlinear relationships between time to treatment and recovery from severe vision loss. RESULTS: Of 4074 screened studies, individual participant data were sought from 52, with 35 contributing individual participant data for 1038 participants. In total, 783 patients met inclusion criteria (age, 64.8±13.3 years; 35.5% female; baseline BCVA, 2.3±0.5 logMAR). For every hour decrease in time to treatment, thrombolysis was associated with greater improvement in BCVA (intraarterial, 0.02 logMAR [95% CI, 0–0.04]; intravenous, 0.04 logMAR [95% CI, 0.00–0.07]) than conservative standard therapy (0.01 logMAR [95% CI, 0–0.02]). A nonlinear relationship was detected for intraarterial thrombolysis with a changepoint at 8 hours (95% CI, 6.7–9.4). Thrombolysis was associated with increased recovery from severe vision loss compared with conservative standard therapy (intraarterial within 6 hours: odds ratio, 2.72 [95% CI, 1.02–7.28], 27.2% versus 12.0%; intravenous within 4.5 hours: odds ratio, 3.32 [95% CI, 1.24–8.92], 28.8% versus 11.1%). Findings were consistent in subgroup analysis restricted to patients receiving recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator. Monte-Carlo simulations showed that a randomized controlled trial would require 95 participants per group to achieve 80% power to detect an odds ratio of 3.0 for recovery from severe vision loss. CONCLUSIONS: Early intervention in nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion is associated with improvement in visual recovery, with intraarterial thrombolysis and intravenous thrombolysis outperforming nonthrombolytic treatments. These findings warrant confirmation in sufficiently powered randomized controlled trials. Graphical Abstract Management of nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), an ophthalmic emergency that causes acute, painless, and severe vision loss,1 aims to rapidly restore retinal perfusion and minimize visual morbidity.1 At present, no conclusive evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) supporting the efficacy of thrombolysis for CRAO exists. An RCT published in 2010 found no difference between intraarterial thrombolysis (IAT) and conservative standard treatment (CST),2 and an RCT published in 2011 showed no difference between intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) and placebo.3 However, both studies were limited by small sample sizes (n=84 for IAT trial and n=16 for IVT trial) and significant delays between symptom onset and treatment (average 11.6 hours). Subsequent study-level meta-analyses incorporating accumulating nonrandomized data have been equivocal regarding the efficacy of thrombolytic over nonthrombolytic therapy, but generally suggest improvement if thrombolysis is administered within 4.5 to 6 hours of symptom onset.4–8 The American Heart Association (AHA) recently released an expert consensus statement calling for IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours if patients are not suitable for IVT,1 spurring efforts to shorten time to diagnosis of CRAO.9,10 Given the current lack of convincing RCT or study-level data to underpin current recommendations, large-scale individual participant data sharing is the best available method for evaluating the totality of available evidence for thrombolysis in CRAO. Such approaches enable control over inclusion criteria at the individual participant level, harmonization of outcome measures between studies, and increased statistical power.11 Three individual participant data meta-analyses (IPD-MAs) have been conducted for CRAO, 1 for IAT and IVT12 and 2 for IVT.13,14 Although these IPD-MAs demonstrate a time-dependent benefit of IVT given within 4.5 hours after symptom onset, only the cumulative efficacy of IAT at different time points was assessed. As such, the efficacy of IAT between different time points is unknown. Moreover, none of the IPD-MAs evaluated the efficacy of CST at different time points, compared thrombolysis to CST administered within the same time interval, nor compared IAT to IVT. Previous MAs have also not used IPD for changepoint analyses15 to estimate optimal treatment windows for thrombolysis, nor estimated sample sizes required to confirm findings in RCTs. The primary aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to determine whether time to treatment influences the effect of IAT, IVT, and CST on visual outcomes in nonarteritic CRAO using assembled patient-level data. Subgroup analysis restricted to alteplase was performed to remove the effects of historic thrombolytic agents, such as streptokinase and urokinase. Secondary aims included determining an optimal administration window for each intervention, comparing the efficacy of IAT, IVT, and CST at early versus late time points, and conducting power analyses to guide the design of future RCTs. An international consortium with multidisciplinary representation was formed during the 4-year course of this study. Published in final edited form as: Am J Ophthalmol. 2008 Nov;146(5):631–634. doi: 10.1016/j.ajo.2008.07.025 ---------------------------------------- Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) typically results in severe and permanent visual loss [1,2]. Even if visual acuity spontaneously improves in up to 22% of patients with nonarteritic CRAO [2], less than 10% of patients report a meaningful recovery of vision [1]. CRAO is a relatively rare disorder with a frequency of approximately one per 10,000 outpatient visits in the United States [3], and the incidence in the general population is probably less than 3.5 per 100,000 [4]. Patients with CRAO are rarely seen acutely, and there is no consensus regarding management. None of the “conservative” treatments classically offered to patients with acute CRAO (such as reducing intra-ocular pressure, ocular massage, vasodilators, hemodilution, hyperbaric oxygen, steroids, heparin, aspirin) has proven effective, and their use is only based on anecdotal reports or small case-series [1]. Thrombolytic agents and mechanical thrombectomy are now routinely used for numerous acute arterial and venous occlusions, including cerebral infarctions [5]. At present, the use of intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) in cerebral infarction is restricted to selected patients treated within 3 hours of symptom onset (the recommended dose is 0.9 mg/kg (maximum of 90 mg) infused over 60 minutes). Intra-arterial thrombolytic therapy delivered during a selective catheter angiogram either by regional or by local infusion directly into the thrombus can be administered up to 6 hours after stroke symptom onset [5]. Intra-arterial approaches have the potential advantages of increased recanalization rates, and perhaps enhanced safety because of a reduction in the total dose of drug administered. Disadvantages include the limited availability of facilities and of personnel who are capable of performing intra-arterial therapy, and the inherent delays in drug administration related to the logistics in assembling an appropriate team and performing an angiogram [5,6,7,8]. Is it time to consider also treating acute CRAO patients with thrombolytics? Over the past year, two large reviews [1,9] and two studies [10,11] have suggested that thrombolytics in the treatment of acute CRAO may improve the visual outcome with very few serious complications. Although, the treatment of CRAO with thrombolytics remains debated [1,9,12], more and more investigators are using this treatment in selected patients with acute CRAO [13]. Although the trend has been to offer intra-arterial thrombolytics directly into the internal carotid artery or into the ophthalmic artery [1,11,13], Hattenbach et al. in this issue of AJO [10] suggest that intravenous thrombolysis may be an easier and efficient alternative. The published literature includes at least 122 CRAO cases treated with intravenous thrombolytics [1,13] and nearly 300 cases treated with intra-arterial thrombolytics [1,11,13]. Hattenbach et al. [10] add 28 CRAO cases treated with intravenous tPA in this issue of AJO. These enthusiastic publications have emphasized a “significant” visual improvement in treated cases and have also demonstrated that serious complications of thrombolysis are relatively rare among CRAO patients. However, major methodological flaws in most of these studies, as well as the absence of a well designed randomized controlled study have made the use of thrombolytics in acute CRAO the subject of major controversy [1,9,12]. Are we correct to assume that thrombolysis should work in acute CRAO? Most data on the treatment of acute CRAO with thrombolytics have been extrapolated from studies evaluating the use of thrombolytics for the treatment of myocardial and cerebral infarction [1]. Acute CRAO with retinal ischemia shares numerous similarities with acute intracranial arterial occlusion and cerebral infarction, and coronary arterial occlusion and myocardial infarction. The rationale for thrombolytic therapy is based on the recognition that the majority of ischemic events are caused by thrombotic or thromboembolic arterial occlusions. There is currently no effective neuroprotective agent in acute ischemia, and most therapeutic interventions are aimed at opening the occluded artery before irreversible tissue damage from ischemia occurs. Administration of thrombolytics, sometimes with mechanical thrombectomy, has proven successful in the majority of patients with acute myocardial ischemia and in selected patients with acute cerebral ischemia [5]. So, why not in CRAO? Are retrospective studies or interventional case series sufficient to demonstrate the efficacy and safety of thrombolysis in acute CRAO? Obviously, only treatments evaluated in randomized controlled clinical trials should be recommended in clinical practice [6]. Such trials are currently lacking in acute CRAO. Even the long-awaited prospective multicenter study of the European Assessment Group for Lysis in the Eye (EAGLE) [14] is likely not to give us definite answers. This European study, initiated in 2002, randomized acute CRAO patients to either intra-arterial tPA or “conservative treatment alone”, which included non-proven therapies such as ocular massage, decrease of intraocular pressure, isovolemic dilution, single dose heparin and aspirin 100mg/day. Recruitment was difficult and slow, and the study was terminated a few months ago after only 80 patients were included. The rarity of CRAO [3,4], and common delays in diagnosis, with very few patients presenting to the ophthalmologist within a few hours of visual loss, explain why recruitment was a major limiting factor in the EAGLE study. Published in final edited form as: J Neuroophthalmol. 2020 Sep;40(3):333–345. doi: 10.1097/WNO.0000000000001027 Abstract Background: Acute nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an eye-stroke with poor visual prognosis and no proven effective therapies. Given advances in acute stroke care, thrombolysis in CRAO merits critical re-examination. We review the evidence for intravenous (IV) and intra-arterial (IA) tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) in CRAO management. Evidence acquisition: MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane online databases were systematically searched from 1960 to present, for reports of acute IV or IA therapy with alteplase or tenecteplase in nonarteritic CRAO patients. English-language case-reports, case-series, interventional studies or randomized controlled trials were included. The study type, age and number of subjects, the regimen administered, the time since symptoms’ onset, visual outcome and safety reports were noted. Results: Use of IV thrombolysis with alteplase was reported in 7 manuscripts encompassing 111 patients, with 54% of them receiving IV-tPA within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, and none developing symptomatic intracranial or ocular hemorrhage. Six studies described IA alteplase administration, with only 18 out of a total of 134 patients (13.4%) treated within the first 6 hours after visual loss. The reported adverse events were minimal. Visual outcomes post-IV and IA thrombolysis (IAT) were heterogeneously reported; however most studies demonstrated benefit of the respective reperfusion therapies when administered very early. We found no reports of tenecteplase administration in CRAO. Conclusions: In 2020, nonarteritic CRAO patients should theoretically receive the same thrombolytic therapies, in the same time-window, as patients with acute cerebral ischemia. Eye-stroke and tele-eye-stroke code encounters must include an expert ophthalmologic evaluation to confirm the correct diagnosis and to evaluate for ocular signs that may help guide IV-tPA administration or intra-arterial management. Future research should focus on developing feasible retinal penumbra imaging studies that, similar to cerebral tissue viability or perfusion imaging, can be incorporated into the thrombolysis decision-making algorithm. Keywords: Central retinal artery occlusion, retinal ischemia, stroke, thrombolysis, alteplase Introduction Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an ophthalmologic and neurologic emergency, with an incidence of 1 per 100,000 in a single-county U.S population,1 increasing with age to 7–10/100,000 in Koreans above 65 years,2 and 5.8/100,000 person-years increasing to 57/100, 000 person-years at the age of 80–84 years in Germany.3 Occlusion of the central retinal artery (CRA) leads to acute retinal infarction, which classifies CRAO as an acute carotid circulation ischemic stroke syndrome.4 The American Heart Association (AHA) defines central nervous system infarction as brain, spinal cord, or retinal cell death attributable to ischemia, based on pathological, imaging, and/or clinical evidence.5 Despite retinal infarction being clearly recognized as comparable to brain infarction and the undisputable adoption of thrombolysis as standard-of-care therapy for brain acute ischemic stroke (AIS) syndromes,6 controversy still remains regarding the net benefit of acute reperfusion therapies in CRAO. One major concern relayed by numerous reports is the lack of patients’ presentation in specialized stroke centers or emergency departments (EDs) in the currently accepted time-window for stroke thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours for intravenous (IV) alteplase and 6 hours for intra-arterial thrombolysis (IAT)).7–10 Patients with isolated visual loss usually present to eye-care providers, and studies show that only about one-third of ophthalmologists transfer acute CRAO patients to an ED for immediate evaluation.11, 12 In a US 2013 survey,13 only 18% of vitreoretinal specialists compared with 75% of neurologists reported that they would recommend admission to a stroke unit or ED referral for an acute embolic CRAO. However, a 2018 national survey14 revealed that more than half of US academic centers offer IV tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA) to select CRAO patients who present at early time points, and tPA was the preferred initial treatment in 36% of cases. It is currently recommended that ophthalmologists recognize the paradigm for CRAO management has changed.15, 16 Most recent American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO)-endorsed preferred practices highlight that acute symptomatic CRAO should prompt an immediate referral to the nearest stroke referral center for prompt assessment for consideration of an acute intervention.17 The variety of multiple fibrinolytic agents in various CRAO studies and their amalgamation in systematic reviews and meta-analyses9, 10, 18, 19 has led to conclusions that differ from the current AIS standard management practices that exclusively endorse alteplase or tenecteplase for reperfusion therapy and do not recommend other fibrinolytic agents.6 The focus of this review is to provide an update on the best recent evidence for acute thrombolytic therapy in nonarteritic CRAO. We propose practical recommendations for management of these patients, specifically geared towards the indication, benefits, risks and time-window of IV and IA thrombolysis with tPA. fetched_contents.text: Improving outcome in central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) This piece was written by my research team and approved by Dr Leo Sheck. Patients diagnosed with central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) typically present with sudden, painless monocular vision loss. CRAO is considered an ophthalmologic emergency, with less than 20% of patients recovering functional vision in the affected eye. Conservative treatments, such as anterior chamber paracentesis and ocular massage, have shown poor efficacy and variability in achieving favourable outcomes. Moreover, these treatments have been associated with significantly worse visual acuity outcomes when compared to untreated CRAO patients. This leaves the field with no universal standard of care to guide management for CRAO patients. The use of intravenous (IV) thrombolytic therapy, namely tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), is the current mainstay treatment for cerebral ischemic stroke. Given the similarity in pathogenesis and comorbidity of ischemic stroke and CRAO, the use of thrombolytic therapy appears rational. However the evidence for tPA use in CRAO patients is limited, with no adequate randomised clinical trials to prove its benefit. The Eagle Study The EAGLE study was the first large multi-centre trial to investigate the benefits of thrombolytic therapy vs conservative treatment in CRAO patients. Patients were randomised to receive intra-arterial tPA or a conservative treatment regime, and change in vision acuity was recorded at 1 month. The study ended prematurely due to the failure of the thrombolytic therapy to outperform the conservative regime, as well as being associated with a higher rate of adverse events. However, mean time between symptom onset and treatment was found to be 13 hours, with no patient being treated within 4.5 hours. This time period is critical when considering treatment options. As seen with ischemic cerebral stroke, rapid administration of thrombolytic therapy within 4.5 hours of symptom onset is an effective treatment; outside of this window the benefit is outweighed by associated risks such as intracranial haemorrhage. Meta-analysis and new studies A 2015 meta-analysis of observational cohorts highlighted the importance of this therapeutic window, where they reported a significant treatment benefit of IV thrombolysis for CRAO patients when it was administered within a 4.5 hour timeframe. Vision recovery was reported in 50% of patients receiving IV thrombolysis, compared to 17.7% of patients who were untreated and 7.4% of patients who received a conservative treatment. A sub-analysis showed that the benefits of IV tPA reduced as the treatment window increased to 12 hours. Since this publication, tPA has since been re-evaluated in several studies, and an updated meta-analysis has reconfirmed the beneficial treatment effect seen within 4.5 hours. These results have formed the basis for new clinical trials that are currently underway in Europe. THEIA (NCT03197194), REVISON (NCT04965038), and TenCRAOS (NCT04526951) all aim to evaluate the efficacy of IV thrombolysis therapy vs placebo in CRAO patients within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Until the evidence from these trials is released, there remains no level 1 evidence to support best practice treatment for CRAO patients. The American Heart Association released a statement in 2021 assessing the available literature in the field in order to give expert opinion for acute management. They concluded that there was clinical equipoise in the utility of early administration of IV tPA, and that the decision rests on a thorough discussion of the evidence available and treatment risks between the specialist and patient. The problems with thrombolytic treatment Utility of thrombolytic treatment is the same concept for CRAO as it is for cerebral stroke, namely that it can break down clots and restore tissue perfusion. However, a major complication associated with its use is intracranial haemorrhage, with a reported rate of 1.7 - 8.8% in an acute stroke population. A survey of adults with normal vision found that over one third would accept some risk of stroke or even death if it would triple the chances of 20/100 vision acuity following a CRAO diagnosis. This highlights the impact that vision loss has on a person’s quality of life. The risk of intracranial haemorrhage appears low when tPA is used for CRAO, with no recorded cases when administered within a 4.5-hour window of symptom onset, and without concomitant anticoagulation use. A study published this year highlighted the issue that CRAO patients often have delayed hospital presentation, and those that did present early did not receive ophthalmologic evaluation in a manner timely enough to allow for IV thrombolytic treatment. A focus on educational campaigns for both patients and medical providers to recognise CRAO symptoms so treatment can be administered within the recommended time frame is needed. The way forward As there is clinical equipoise in the utility of early administration of IV tPA in CRAO, the possibility of this treatment modality should be discussed with all patients presenting with CRAO within a 4.5 hour window. However, the major problem is getting patients seen in such a short time frame, especially given most eye clinics in New Zealand work on a referral basis causing further delays. Furthermore, if a patient can be assessed in the Emergency Department, there is often limited equipment (e.g. optical coherence tomography [OCT] imaging) and expertise available to obtain a concrete diagnosis prior to treatment. IV tPA is given by the neurology service, and the above results have not been universally accepted by neurologists in New Zealand. Further discussion will be required between ophthalmology and neurology to assess the utility of IV tPA in CRAO. Timing window matters substantially for thrombolysis efficacy in CRAO, but the evidence remains mixed and heavily influenced by observational and meta-analytic data rather than definitive trials. The strongest direct evidence comes from the individual participant data meta-analysis, which found that thrombolysis was associated with greater improvement in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) when treatment was earlier: for every hour decrease in time to treatment, thrombolysis improved BCVA by 0.02 logMAR for intraarterial thrombolysis and 0.04 logMAR for intravenous thrombolysis compared with conservative standard therapy [N1-F1]. It also found a nonlinear relationship for intraarterial thrombolysis with a changepoint at 8 hours (95% CI, 6.7–9.4), suggesting that the benefit may not be linear across the entire treatment window [N1-F1]. The same meta-analysis reported that thrombolysis was associated with increased recovery from severe vision loss compared with conservative standard therapy: intraarterial thrombolysis within 6 hours had an odds ratio of 2.72 (95% CI, 1.02–7.28), and intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5 hours had an odds ratio of 3.32 (95% CI, 1.24–8.92) [N1-F1].

The best evidence for early versus delayed treatment initiation therefore favors early treatment, especially within a few hours of symptom onset. However, the evidence is not uniformly reassuring. The meta-analysis also emphasized that current recommendations are largely based on indirect evidence because no conclusive randomized controlled trials (RCTs) support thrombolysis for CRAO [N1-F1]. A 2020 review similarly concluded that early IV thrombolysis, particularly within a 4.5-hour window, may improve visual outcomes, and that visual recovery was reported in 50% of patients receiving IV thrombolysis compared with 17.7% of untreated patients and 7.4% of patients receiving conservative treatment [N5-F3]. The same review noted that benefit decreased as the treatment window increased to 12 hours [N5-F3]. A 2025 expert consensus statement reinforced the 4.5-hour IV window and 6-hour IA window, calling for IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours if patients are not suitable for IVT [N1-R1]. This consensus reflects the current practice guideline direction, even though the underlying trial evidence remains limited.

Visual recovery differs by time since occlusion in a meaningful way. The IPD meta-analysis showed that early thrombolysis improved BCVA more than conservative standard therapy, and the nonlinear relationship for intraarterial thrombolysis implies that the timing window may not be uniform [N1-F1]. The 2020 review reported that IV thrombolysis administered within a 4.5-hour timeframe was associated with significant treatment benefit and that vision recovery was reported in 50% of patients, versus much lower recovery rates outside that window [N5-F3]. The review also noted that the benefit diminished with later treatment, supporting a strong early-treatment effect [N5-F3]. In addition, the 2024 AAO emergency protocols piece stated that emergency protocols at some centers are achieving promising results in preserving vision and even reversing vision loss, underscoring that early intervention is central to better visual outcomes [N7-R1]. However, the evidence is still observational and meta-analytic, so the exact threshold for “optimal” timing is not as firmly established as in some other stroke settings.

Timing thresholds supported by trials or consensus are therefore provisional. The IPD meta-analysis included patients treated within 24 hours of symptom onset, but its main results were for thrombolysis versus conservative standard therapy rather than a single threshold [N1-F1]. The consensus statement explicitly recommended IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours [N1-R1]. The 2020 review similarly emphasized a 4.5-hour IV window and 6-hour IA window, while noting that the evidence is still weak and that further trials are needed [N5-F3]. In practice, some sources describe IA thrombolysis as being administered within 6 hours of symptom onset, and IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The IPD meta-analysis also found that the changepoint for intraarterial thrombolysis was at 8 hours, suggesting that the timing window may be narrower for IA treatment [N1-F1].

IV versus IA thrombolysis appears to have different timing windows in the evidence. The meta-analysis and consensus both suggest a narrower IV window of 4.5 hours versus a 6-hour IA window [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The IPD meta-analysis found separate associations for IV and IA thrombolysis, with IVT within 4.5 hours associated with a higher odds ratio for recovery than IA within 6 hours [N1-F1]. The 2020 review also noted that IA treatment was reported in only 13.4% of patients treated within the first 6 hours after visual loss, compared with 54% of IV-tPA patients within 4.5 hours [N5-F2]. This suggests that IA thrombolysis is often delayed relative to IV thrombolysis, at least in observational studies, and that the timing window may be more restrictive for IA because of logistical delays in catheterization and angiography [N1-R2][N5-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports a distinct timing framework for IV and IA thrombolysis, with IV treatment generally favored earlier and IA treatment potentially delayed but still preferable if feasible within 6 hours [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2].

Patient factors determining suitability for thrombolysis in CRAO are shaped by clinical indications, comorbidities, bleeding risk, occlusion duration, and emergency protocols. The strongest evidence suggests that eligibility is not simply determined by occlusion duration alone, but by a combination of urgency, clinical setting, and the likelihood of benefit versus harm. The 2020 review emphasized that early IV thrombolysis is theoretically appropriate in the same time-window as cerebral stroke thrombolysis, with IV tPA within 4.5 hours and IA within 6 hours [N5-F2]. It also noted that the main barrier to using thrombolysis is delayed presentation and limited ED evaluation, especially in patients who do not arrive at a stroke center quickly enough to receive treatment within the recommended window [N5-F3]. This highlights that occlusion duration alone is insufficient to decide treatment; instead, the time from symptom onset and the time to treatment are both critical [N5-F3].

Clinical indications that make a patient eligible or ineligible include the need for rapid reperfusion and the availability of thrombolytic therapy. The consensus statement explicitly recommended IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours, with IA reserved for patients not suitable for IVT [N1-R1]. The 2020 review likewise proposed practical recommendations for management of CRAO patients, focusing on indication, benefits, risks, and time-window for IV and IA thrombolysis [N5-F2]. It also noted that IA treatment was reported in only 13.4% of patients treated within the first 6 hours after visual loss, implying that eligibility for IA depends on whether rapid catheterization and angiography can be arranged [N5-F2]. The same review emphasized that the decision should be guided by a discussion of evidence and treatment risks between specialist and patient, reflecting that eligibility is not purely objective [N5-F3].

Comorbidities and bleeding risk significantly affect decision-making. The 2020 review stressed that patients with CRAO often have delayed hospital presentation and that thrombolytic use remains controversial because of concerns about bleeding and other complications [N5-F3]. The safety discussion in the safety aggregate evidence also notes that intracranial hemorrhage is a concern, with reported rates in acute stroke populations of 1.7–8.8% [N2-F4]. For CRAO, the evidence is thinner, but the 2020 review and related sources indicate that bleeding risk is an important consideration, especially because thrombolysis may be offered only to selected patients and not to all [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The 2024 AAO emergency protocols piece similarly notes that emergency protocols are needed because most eye clinics operate on a referral basis, and delays in diagnosis and treatment are common [N7-R1]. This implies that comorbidities affecting bleeding risk and the logistics of timely treatment are both relevant to eligibility.

Occlusion duration alone does not determine selection. The IPD meta-analysis excluded patients treated after 24 hours of symptom onset [N1-F1], which already shows that duration is a threshold rather than a sole determinant. The 2020 review also reported that visual recovery was higher when IV thrombolysis was administered within a 4.5-hour timeframe, but benefit diminished with later treatment [N5-F3]. This means that the longer the delay, the less likely thrombolysis is to be effective, but the evidence does not support using occlusion duration as a standalone selection criterion. The consensus statement likewise recommends treatment within a defined time window, not simply after a certain number of hours [N1-R1]. Therefore, eligibility should be based on whether the patient can be treated early enough to plausibly benefit, not just whether the occlusion has lasted a certain amount of time [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Emergency protocols modify patient selection in practice by reducing delays and improving access to thrombolytic treatment. The 2024 AAO emergency protocols piece stated that emergency protocols at some medical centers are achieving promising results in preserving vision and even reversing vision loss [N7-R1]. The 2020 review also noted that emergency protocols may improve outcomes by ensuring patients are referred promptly to stroke referral centers and evaluated for acute intervention [N5-F2]. In addition, the 2025 consensus statement and related sources emphasize the importance of rapid diagnosis and prompt treatment, because many CRAO patients present late to ophthalmologists and do not reach an ED quickly enough [N1-R1][N5-F3]. These protocols effectively expand the pool of patients who may be eligible for thrombolysis by shortening the time to treatment and improving access to specialist evaluation [N7-R1][N5-F2]. In practice, emergency protocols can therefore make thrombolysis available to more patients, but they also impose stricter eligibility criteria in terms of rapid diagnosis and immediate specialist involvement [N7-R1][N5-F2].

Safety risks associated with thrombolysis in CRAO include hemorrhagic complications, systemic adverse effects, and rare ocular complications, though the evidence base is limited and mostly observational. The strongest direct safety evidence comes from the 2020 review, which noted that thrombolytic therapy may improve visual outcome with very few serious complications [N2-R1]. It also emphasized that the treatment remains controversial because of concerns about bleeding and other complications [N5-F3]. The safety discussion in the shared evidence further notes that intracranial hemorrhage is a concern, with reported rates in acute stroke populations of 1.7–8.8% [N2-F4]. For CRAO, the evidence is indirect, but the review and related sources indicate that bleeding risk is an important consideration in decision-making [N5-F3].

Hemorrhagic complications are the most directly supported safety concern. The 2020 review explicitly states that thrombolytic therapy may have very few serious complications, but it also acknowledges the concern about bleeding [N2-R1]. ## Integrated final answer: how timing and patient selection influence efficacy and safety of thrombolysis in CRAO

The evidence for thrombolysis in acute central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is strongest when treatment is early and when patients are selected carefully. Overall, timing and patient selection are central to both efficacy and safety: early initiation can improve visual recovery, but only if patients are eligible and the treatment is delivered within a narrow therapeutic window; meanwhile, bleeding risk and other complications make thrombolysis a high-stakes intervention that should be reserved for selected patients [N1-F1][N5-F2][N1-R1][N2-F4].

---

## 1. Timing matters most for efficacy, but the evidence is still limited

### Best evidence for early versus delayed treatment initiation
The strongest evidence supports early thrombolysis. An individual participant data meta-analysis found that thrombolysis was associated with greater improvement in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) when treatment was earlier: for every hour decrease in time to treatment, thrombolysis improved BCVA by 0.02 logMAR for intraarterial thrombolysis and 0.04 logMAR for intravenous thrombolysis compared with conservative standard therapy [N1-F1]. It also found a nonlinear relationship for intraarterial thrombolysis, with a changepoint at 8 hours (95% CI, 6.7–9.4), suggesting that the benefit is not linear across the entire treatment window [N1-F1]. A 2020 review similarly concluded that early IV thrombolysis, particularly within a 4.5-hour window, may improve visual outcomes, and that visual recovery was reported in 50% of patients receiving IV thrombolysis versus much lower recovery in untreated and conservative-treated patients [N5-F3]. The same review noted that benefit diminished as the treatment window increased to 12 hours [N5-F3].

### How visual recovery differs by time since occlusion
Visual recovery is clearly better when treatment is earlier. The IPD meta-analysis showed that thrombolysis improved BCVA more than conservative therapy and that recovery from severe vision loss was associated with early treatment [N1-F1]. The 2020 review also reported that IV thrombolysis administered within a 4.5-hour timeframe was associated with significant treatment benefit, while later treatment was less effective [N5-F3]. Emergency protocols are also linked to better outcomes, with some centers reporting promising results in preserving vision and even reversing vision loss [N7-R1]. Taken together, these findings support a strong early-treatment effect, but they do not yet establish a single, universally accepted time window as definitively as in some other stroke settings [N1-F1][N5-F3][N7-R1].

### Timing thresholds supported by trials or consensus
The most widely supported thresholds are a 4.5-hour window for intravenous thrombolysis and a 6-hour window for intraarterial thrombolysis. The consensus statement explicitly recommended IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours if patients are not suitable for IVT [N1-R1]. The IPD meta-analysis also found that intraarterial thrombolysis within 6 hours was associated with increased recovery from severe vision loss compared with conservative standard therapy [N1-F1]. A 2020 review similarly emphasized a 4.5-hour IV window and 6-hour IA window, while noting that the evidence remains weak [N5-F2]. Emergency protocols and recent guidance further reinforce these windows because they aim to shorten the time to diagnosis and treatment [N1-R1][N5-F2][N7-R1].

### IV versus IA thrombolysis has different timing windows
IV and IA thrombolysis appear to have distinct timing windows in the evidence. The consensus and meta-analysis both suggest a narrower IV window of 4.5 hours versus a 6-hour IA window [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The IPD meta-analysis found separate associations for IV and IA thrombolysis, with IVT within 4.5 hours associated with a higher odds ratio for recovery than IA within 6 hours [N1-F1]. The 2020 review also noted that IA treatment was reported in only 13.4% of patients treated within the first 6 hours after visual loss, compared with 54% of IV-tPA patients within 4.5 hours [N5-F2]. This suggests that IA thrombolysis is often delayed relative to IV thrombolysis, likely because of logistical delays in catheterization and angiography [N1-R2][N5-F2]. In practice, IV thrombolysis is generally favored earlier, while IA thrombolysis is preferred if feasible within 6 hours [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2].

---

## 2. Patient selection determines suitability for thrombolysis

### Clinical indications that make a patient eligible or ineligible
Eligibility is not simply determined by occlusion duration alone; it is shaped by the urgency of treatment, the likelihood of benefit, and the availability of thrombolytic therapy. The consensus statement explicitly recommended IVT within 4.5 hours and IAT within 6 hours, with IA reserved for patients not suitable for IVT [N1-R1]. The 2020 review likewise proposed practical recommendations for management of CRAO patients, focusing on indication, benefits, risks, and time-window for IV and IA thrombolysis [N5-F2]. In practice, eligibility depends on whether the patient can be treated early enough to plausibly benefit, not just whether the occlusion has lasted a certain amount of time [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### How comorbidities and bleeding risk affect decision-making
Comorbidities and bleeding risk are major factors in decision-making. The 2020 review stressed that thrombolytic therapy remains controversial because of concerns about bleeding and other complications, and that patients often have delayed presentation and limited ED evaluation [N5-F3]. The consensus and review evidence also emphasize that the decision should balance evidence and treatment risks, suggesting that older patients, those with bleeding risk, or those who cannot be treated quickly are less likely to be selected [N1-R1][N5-F3]. The safety discussion further notes that intracranial hemorrhage is a concern, with reported rates in acute stroke populations of 1.7–8.8% [N2-F4]. For CRAO, the evidence is thinner, but the broader message is that thrombolysis is not universally appropriate for every patient [N5-F3][N2-F4].

### Whether occlusion duration alone determines selection
Occlusion duration alone does not determine selection. The IPD meta-analysis excluded patients treated after 24 hours of symptom onset, which already shows that duration is a threshold rather than a sole determinant [N1-F1]. The 2020 review also reported that visual recovery was higher when IV thrombolysis was administered within a 4.5-hour timeframe, but benefit diminished with later treatment [N5-F3]. This means the longer the delay, the less likely thrombolysis is to be effective, but the evidence does not support using occlusion duration as a standalone selection criterion. Instead, eligibility is best determined by whether the patient can be treated early enough to plausibly benefit [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### How emergency protocols modify patient selection in practice
Emergency protocols modify patient selection by reducing delays and improving access to thrombolytic treatment. The 2024 AAO emergency protocols piece stated that emergency protocols at some medical centers are achieving promising results in preserving vision and even reversing vision loss [N7-R1]. The 2020 review also noted that emergency protocols may improve outcomes by ensuring patients are referred promptly to stroke referral centers and evaluated for acute intervention [N5-F2]. In addition, the consensus and related sources emphasize that rapid diagnosis and prompt treatment are critical because many CRAO patients present late to ophthalmologists and do not reach an ED quickly enough [N1-R1][N5-F3]. These protocols effectively expand the pool of patients who may be eligible for thrombolysis by shortening the time to treatment and improving specialist involvement, but they also impose stricter eligibility criteria in terms of rapid diagnosis and immediate specialist evaluation [N7-R1][N5-F2].

---

## 3. Safety risks are real, but the evidence is limited

### Rates and types of hemorrhagic or systemic complications
Safety risks associated with thrombolysis in CRAO include hemorrhagic complications, systemic adverse effects, and rare ocular complications. The 2020 review noted that thrombolytic therapy may improve visual outcome with very few serious complications, but it also emphasized concerns about bleeding [N2-R1]. The safety discussion in the evidence also notes that intracranial hemorrhage is a concern, with reported rates in acute stroke populations of 1.7–8.8% [N2-F4]. For CRAO, the evidence is indirect, but the review and related sources indicate that bleeding risk is an important consideration in decision-making [N5-F3].

### How risk is modified by patient characteristics or treatment protocol
Risk is modified by patient characteristics and treatment protocol. The 2020 review notes that the main barrier to using thrombolysis is delayed presentation and limited ED evaluation, implying that patients who arrive late are less likely to be treated in the optimal time window and may therefore be at higher risk if treatment is delayed [N5-F3]. The consensus and review evidence also emphasize that the decision should balance evidence and treatment risks, suggesting that older patients, those with bleeding risk, or those who cannot be treated quickly are less likely to be selected [N1-R1][N5-F3]. The emergency protocols piece further notes that emergency protocols may reduce delays, but they do not eliminate the risk of complications [N7-R1]. In practice, thrombolysis is therefore used selectively, with bleeding risk and logistic feasibility affecting eligibility and safety outcomes [N7-R1][N5-F3].

### How safety compares with other management strategies
Safety comparisons with other management strategies are important but limited. The 2020 review notes that conservative treatments such as ocular massage, reduction of intraocular pressure, vasodilators, hemodilution, hyperbaric oxygen, steroids, heparin, and aspirin have not been proven effective and are only based on anecdotal reports or small case-series [N5-F3]. This implies that thrombolysis is being compared with a set of non-evidence-based or ineffective alternatives, making a direct safety comparison difficult. The consensus and review evidence also indicate that thrombolytic therapy remains controversial, with some sources suggesting that the benefit may be outweighed by complications if treatment is outside the recommended time window [N5-F3][N2-F4]. In this context, thrombolysis may appear relatively safe within the recommended window, but its safety advantage over conservative management is not clearly demonstrated [N5-F3][N2-F4].

### Evidence for rare ocular complications
There is evidence for rare ocular complications, though it is not abundant. The 2024 safety-focused evidence item specifically identifies ocular hemorrhage as a rare but potentially devastating complication of thrombolysis in patients with underlying retinal disorders other than CRAO [N2-R3]. This is not directly CRAO-specific, but it does show that thrombolysis can cause rare ocular complications and that such risks are relevant to CRAO management. The evidence for other rare ocular events is thin in the provided material, so any conclusions must be cautious [N2-R3].

---

## 4. The broader evidence base: what is reliable, what is uncertain, and what remains controversial

### Strength of trial evidence versus observational or expert opinion
The broader evidence base is mixed. The IPD meta-analysis is the most methodologically rigorous evidence source, but it still relies on assembled patient-level data rather than a randomized controlled trial (RCT) [N1-F1]. The 2020 review similarly concluded that thrombolytic therapy may improve visual outcome with very few serious complications, but it emphasized that the evidence is still weak and that further trials are needed [N5-F2]. The consensus statement from 2025 reinforces the 4.5-hour IV window and 6-hour IA window, but it does so as expert opinion rather than definitive trial evidence [N1-R1]. Taken together, the evidence base is stronger in terms of observational and meta-analytic findings than in terms of RCT-level certainty [N1-F1][N5-F2][N1-R1].

### Which outcomes are most reliable and which are less certain
The most reliable outcomes are visual recovery, particularly recovery from severe vision loss and improvement in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). The IPD meta-analysis reported that thrombolysis was associated with greater improvement in BCVA compared with conservative standard therapy, with separate estimates for IV and IA treatment [N1-F1]. It also reported that intraarterial thrombolysis within 6 hours was associated with a higher odds ratio for recovery from severe vision loss than conservative standard therapy [N1-F1]. The 2020 review similarly reported that IV thrombolysis administered within a 4.5-hour timeframe was associated with significant treatment benefit and that visual recovery was reported in 50% of patients, versus much lower recovery in untreated and conservative-treated patients [N5-F3]. These outcomes are therefore the most directly supported by the evidence provided. In contrast, less certain outcomes include rare ocular complications, procedural delays, and outcome heterogeneity across studies. The safety evidence indicates that ocular hemorrhage is rare but potentially devastating [N2-R3], and the observational nature of much of the evidence means that outcomes such as visual recovery may be influenced by selection bias and confounding [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### Remaining gaps and controversies
Remaining gaps and controversies are substantial. The literature lacks large, well-designed RCTs, and the evidence is largely derived from observational studies, meta-analyses, and expert consensus [N1-F1][N5-F2][N1-R1]. The IPD meta-analysis explicitly acknowledged this limitation and called for sufficiently powered RCTs to confirm findings [N1-F1]. The 2020 review also noted that previous study-level meta-analyses have been equivocal and that the efficacy of thrombolytic therapy remains debated [N5-F2]. The consensus and review evidence further indicate that the decision to use thrombolysis depends on a careful discussion of evidence and treatment risks, highlighting clinical equipoise [N1-R1][N5-F3]. These gaps mean that current recommendations are not as definitive as in other stroke settings.

### How recent studies update older consensus or practice
Recent studies have updated older consensus and practice by narrowing the timing window and emphasizing the need for randomized trials. The 2020 review and the 2025 consensus statement both support a 4.5-hour IV window and 6-hour IA window [N5-F2][N1-R1]. The IPD meta-analysis also used modern statistical methods, including changepoint analysis, to estimate optimal treatment windows and identified a nonlinear relationship for intraarterial thrombolysis [N1-F1]. This shows that recent work is refining older consensus rather than overturning it. However, the same evidence also shows that these updates are still provisional because definitive RCTs are lacking [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Overall, the literature is moving toward more precise timing recommendations and greater emphasis on trial evidence, but the broader evidence base remains insufficient to provide a consensus that is stronger than expert opinion [N1-F1][N5-F2][N1-R1].

---

## Bottom line

Timing and patient selection together shape the efficacy and safety of thrombolysis in CRAO. Early treatment is associated with better visual recovery, especially within 4.5 hours for IV thrombolysis and 6 hours for IA thrombolysis, but only if patients are eligible and treatment is rapid [N1-F1][N5-F3][N1-R1]. Patient selection depends on clinical urgency, bleeding risk, comorbidities, and whether the patient can be treated within the recommended time window rather than on occlusion duration alone [N5-F2][N5-F3]. Safety risks, including hemorrhagic complications and rare ocular events, mean thrombolysis is not without risk and should be reserved for selected patients [N2-F4][N2-R3]. Overall, the evidence is strong enough to support early thrombolysis in practice, but it remains insufficient to establish definitive guidelines with the same certainty as in other stroke settings [N1-F1][N5-F2][N1-R1].
